8. Blocks, permutations, and elementary operations

8.1 Partitioned multiplication

A block matrix groups contiguous entries into rectangular submatrices. The block entries may themselves be nonsquare. Treating them like scalars is safe only when every product and sum has compatible shape and factor order is preserved.

[A11A12A21A22] [B11B12B21B22] = [A11B11+A12B21A11B12+A12B22A21B11+A22B21A21B12+A22B22].

Suppose the A row partition has sizes r and s, and its column partition sizes u and v. The B row partition must have those same sizes u and v. If B's column partition has sizes t and w, then A12 is r-by-v, B21 is v-by-t, and both terms in the top-left sum are r-by-t. Matching only the number of blocks is insufficient; the intermediate block widths and heights must match too.

The block rule follows by splitting the shared-index sum into ranges. There is no new multiplication operation. It is the usual operation reorganized around structural groups. A block diagonal product multiplies corresponding diagonal blocks, while zero off-diagonal blocks remove other terms.

For compatible blocks a useful inverse identity is:

[IX0I]−1 = [I−X0I].

The identities can have different sizes and X can be rectangular. Both products give the appropriate block identity. More general block inverse formulas require additional invertibility assumptions and will be studied with elimination; inverses of individual blocks cannot simply be taken entrywise.

8.2 Permutations act on a particular side

A permutation matrix has exactly one one in each row and column and zeros elsewhere. Its columns are permuted standard basis vectors, so they are orthonormal and P−1 = PT. Left multiplication PA reorders rows. Right multiplication AP reorders columns according to P's columns. The two reorderings need not have the same index convention.

For a simple swap of two coordinates the same matrix performs its own inverse, but a three-cycle does not. If P maps e1 to e2, e2 to e3, and e3 to e1, then AP has columns a2, a3, a1, whereas PA has rows row 3, row 1, row 2. Derive the side-specific effect instead of transferring a verbal permutation blindly.

8.3 Row additions as matrix multiplication

For i ≠ j, E = I+αeiejT adds α times row j to row i when it multiplies on the left. The outer product selects row j and places it into row i. Because (eiejT)2 = 0, the inverse is I−αeiejT. On the right, the same matrix adds α times column i to column j. The input and output roles reverse across the side.

This is the algebraic basis of elementary row operations. The next chapter organizes these operations into Gaussian elimination; here the emphasis is knowing exactly which coordinates a multiplication changes and how the operation is undone.

9. Trace, Frobenius geometry, and useful extensions

9.1 Trace and cyclic order

The trace of a square matrix is the sum of its diagonal entries. It is linear and unchanged by transposition. If A is m-by-n and B is n-by-m, both AB and BA are square, possibly of different sizes, and:

tr(AB) = ∑i=1m ∑k=1n aikbki = tr(BA).

Interchange the two finite sums to prove the last equality. This does not say AB = BA. It says one scalar statistic agrees. For a compatible cyclic product, trace is unchanged by rotating the entire factor sequence, for example tr(ABC) = tr(BCA) = tr(CAB). Arbitrarily swapping two adjacent factors is not a cyclic rotation and can change the trace.

If S is invertible, tr(S−1AS) = tr(A), by one cyclic rotation and cancellation. This is a useful bridge to later similarity theory, but no eigenvalue claim is needed to prove it.

9.2 Frobenius norm and orthogonal invariance

The Frobenius norm treats the matrix entries as a vector:

‖A‖F2 = ∑i=1m ∑j=1n aij2 = tr(ATA).

It also equals the sum of squared column lengths and the sum of squared row lengths. For complex matrices replace squared entries by squared moduli and use tr(A∗A). The Frobenius inner product is tr(ATB) over the real field; expanding the trace gives the sum of aijbij.

Left multiplication by an orthogonal Q preserves each column length, so ‖QA‖F = ‖A‖F. Right multiplication by an orthogonal R preserves each row length, yielding ‖AR‖F = ‖A‖F. Alternatively substitute into the trace formula and use the cyclic law. Symmetric and skew-symmetric parts are orthogonal under this matrix inner product: paired off-diagonal terms cancel, and the skew part's diagonal is zero. Hence ‖A‖F2 = ‖H‖F2+‖K‖F2.

For compatible A and B, scalar Cauchy–Schwarz on each output entry gives |(AB)ij|2 ≤ (sum of squares in row i of A)(sum of squares in column j of B). Summing over i and j separates the factors and proves ‖AB‖F ≤ ‖A‖F‖B‖F. This bound is valid but can be loose; it is not a claim that every factor changes all lengths by its Frobenius norm.

9.3 Hadamard and Kronecker products

The Hadamard product A ⊙ B multiplies corresponding entries and requires identical shapes. It is commutative over ℝ or ℂ, unlike ordinary multiplication. For a fixed same-shape pair, the Hadamard product and AB can both exist yet be different. An examination problem must identify which product it means.

The Kronecker product A ⊗ B replaces entry aij by the block aijB. If A is m-by-n and B p-by-q, its shape is mp-by-nq. For compatible pairs A,C and B,D:

(A⊗B)(C⊗D) = (AC)⊗(BD).

To verify it, label a row by (i,r) and a column by (j,s). The product entry sums aikbrtckjdts over k and t. Scalar commutation separates this into (sum over k of aikckj)(sum over t of brtdts), giving the stated block entry. The rule preserves the order within AC and within BD.

These products are included to remove notation ambiguity, not to assume advanced tensor theory. Ordinary multiplication remains the default everywhere else in the chapter.

Animated concept walkthrough

The matrix entries are one, two, three and four in row-major order. Its trace is five, while its squared Frobenius norm is thirty.

Choose a concept, then use Play, Next step, Previous step, or the checkpoint slider. Every stop includes its exact state and a complete explanation.

Add the square of the next matrix entry to the Frobenius-norm total. Diagonal trace and total entry-square mass are different matrix summaries.

Model condition. The trace sums diagonal entries; the Frobenius norm squares and sums every entry.

10. Computation, operation counts, and perturbations

10.1 An exact reference algorithm

The following pseudocode uses zero-based array positions but computes the same mathematical product. Explicitly initializing the accumulator prevents old values from contaminating entries.

multiply(A, B):
    m, n = shape(A)
    r, p = shape(B)
    require n == r
    C = zero_matrix(m, p)
    for i in 0 .. m-1:
        for j in 0 .. p-1:
            total = 0
            for k in 0 .. n-1:
                total = total + A[i,k] * B[k,j]
            C[i,j] = total
    return C

For each output entry the algorithm multiplies n pairs and performs n additions if adding the first product to an initial zero is counted. A minimal scalar arithmetic count uses n−1 additions by assigning the first product to the accumulator. Therefore dense multiplication costs mnp multiplications and mp(n−1) minimal additions. When counting multiply-and-add pairs or machine instructions, state the convention separately. Dense square multiplication by this algorithm has cubic time and quadratic output storage; the full storage also includes the inputs.

This count applies to the classical algorithm. It is not a lower bound for all matrix multiplication algorithms. Sparsity, special structure, and faster general algorithms change the cost. Exact rational arithmetic also has bit costs that this scalar-operation count does not capture.

10.2 Parenthesization changes cost, not factor order

Let A be 10-by-100, B 100-by-5, and C 5-by-50. Computing (AB)C costs 5,000+2,500 = 7,500 scalar multiplications. Computing A(BC) costs 25,000+50,000 = 75,000. Both results are 10-by-50 and equal in exact arithmetic. The first route makes a small intermediate matrix; the second a large one. Associativity allows the cheaper route but does not allow reordering A, B, C.

For a longer chain with dimensions d0,…,dr, the matrix-chain dynamic-programming recurrence is:

M(i,j) = mini≤k<j {M(i,k)+M(k+1,j)+di−1dkdj},   M(i,i) = 0.

Every final split divides the chain into a left and right subchain; after their products are computed, the final multiplication has the displayed dimension cost. Enumerating all splits and solving shorter chains first proves the recurrence finds the smallest classical multiplication count. This is an algebra–algorithms connection; it does not require implementing the optimizer during this study session.

10.3 Exact identities and floating-point behavior

Mathematical associativity does not guarantee bit-identical floating-point results. Scalar additions are rounded, and regrouping changes which intermediate numbers are rounded. For example, with finite precision, adding a tiny value to a huge one can discard the tiny value, while subtracting the huge values first can preserve it. Avoid interpreting a small computed discrepancy as a failure of the algebraic theorem.

For perturbed inputs A+E and B+F, exact distributivity gives:

(A+E)(B+F)−AB = AF+EB+EF.

The Frobenius product bound and triangle inequality imply a quantitative error bound:

‖(A+E)(B+F)−AB‖F ≤ ‖A‖F‖F‖F + ‖E‖F‖B‖F + ‖E‖F‖F‖F.

For small perturbations the first two terms dominate, but the quadratic term is present in the exact identity. Dropping it requires declaring an approximation. This is a useful habit for every later numerical method: distinguish a mathematical identity, a computational approximation, and an empirical observation.

11. Interactive laboratory: order of transformations

Choose a shear and a rotation, then compare their two composition orders on the same input vector. The blue result applies the shear first and the rotation second. The amber result applies the rotation first and the shear second. The dashed outline is the original unit square; the colored outlines are its images. The grid uses the same scale on both axes.

11.1 What to inspect

First set the shear to zero: both orders reduce to the same rotation. Next set the rotation to zero: both reduce to the same shear. With a half-turn, the rotation is −I, which commutes with every matrix, so the orders agree again. With a quarter-turn and nonzero shear they differ. Changing the input can reveal whether two different matrices happen to agree on that particular vector.

The displayed matrix difference is the commutator RS−SR. For s ≠ 0 and sin(θ) ≠ 0 it has nonzero diagonal entries of opposite sign, so these two particular maps disagree on every nonzero input. For other matrix pairs a nonzero commutator can still annihilate some nonzero vectors; the laboratory's conclusion should not be generalized without a proof. The squared difference of output coordinates is computed directly, not inferred from picture overlap.

The shapes of transformed squares reveal why a shear is not generally length-preserving. A pure rotation preserves side lengths and angles; a shear changes the square into a parallelogram. Both preserve the origin and linear combinations. A picture illustrates these facts; the formulas establish them.

Teaching through formulas and conceptual decisions

Make shape and factor order part of every calculation

If A is m×k and B is k×n, then (AB)ij=∑r=1kAirBrj and the output has shape m×n. Row-column pairing fixes the answer. Composition applies the rightmost factor first to column vectors. Associativity permits changing parentheses, not changing factor order. A transpose or inverse reverses product order: (AB)T=BTAT and (AB)−1=B−1A−1 when both square factors are invertible.

Calculate operation counts from shapes

The ordinary product of m×k and k×n matrices uses mkn scalar multiplications and mn(k−1) additions if each dot product starts from its first product. Parenthesizing a chain changes intermediate shapes and work. For shapes 10×100, 100×5, 5×50, the left association uses 5000+2500=7500 multiplications; the right uses 25000+50000=75000. Both yield the same exact mathematical matrix while their computational cost differs by a factor 10.

Exploit structure without assuming cancellation

For A=I+N with N2=0, the inverse is I−N because their product is I−N2=I. For a nilpotent N of index r, the finite geometric inverse has alternating powers through r−1. A scalar cancellation rule cannot justify matrix cancellation: nonzero matrices can multiply to zero. Left cancellation requires an injective left action, while right cancellation requires a suitable right-side condition. Square invertibility supplies both.

The Gram matrix ATA satisfies xTATAx=|Ax|2≥0. It is positive definite precisely when A has independent columns. Orthonormal columns imply ATA=I, but a tall rectangular A cannot also satisfy AAT=I on the larger space. The latter product is a projection onto its column space.

Detailed derivation tutorials

The following complete proofs and implementations support the new examination problems. They develop the reasoning needed to derive formulas; the separately labeled examination bank below tests calculation, concepts and distractor decisions.

Reading instruction. These are teaching examples with complete solutions, not a test of material you have not yet studied. Read the reasoning and the final lesson together. The progression moves from shape checks to structural proofs and advanced connections. Problems marked course-derived adapt a mathematical problem type with newly written explanations; they do not reproduce an entire source exercise collection. All remaining questions are original.

Tutorial 1 — Diagnose dimensions before calculating

Let A be 2-by-3, B 3-by-4, C 4-by-2, and D 2-by-2. Determine the shapes of AB, BA, ABC, CAB, A+B, DA, and AD. Explain every undefined expression.

Solution. AB contracts the matching inner dimension three and leaves shape 2-by-4. BA would need four, the number of columns of B, to equal two, the number of rows of A; it is undefined. ABC is defined in either grouping: AB is 2-by-4 and can multiply C, giving 2-by-2; BC is 3-by-2 and can be premultiplied by A, with the same output shape. CAB is 4-by-4, because CA is 4-by-3 and then multiplies B. Addition A+B is undefined because both dimensions must match. DA is 2-by-3, while AD is undefined because three does not match two.

The cyclic order changed the final shape from 2-by-2 for ABC to 4-by-4 for CAB. That does not contradict trace cyclicity: their traces can agree even though their sizes differ. Lesson: compatible multiplication contracts an intermediate dimension; addition never contracts dimensions.

Tutorial 2 — Recover a matrix from linear combinations

Suppose X+2Y = [5014] and 3X−Y = [1710−2]. Find X and Y without solving four separate systems.

Solution. Call the right sides M and N. Multiplying the first equation by three and subtracting the second gives 7Y = 3M−N. Therefore Y = (3M−N)/7 = 17[14−7−714] = [2−1−12]. Substitute into the first equation: X = M−2Y = [1230]. Verification in the second equation gives 3X−Y = [1710−2], as required.

This manipulation is valid because matrix addition and scalar multiplication obey vector-space laws. It does not divide by a matrix or commute any matrix factors. Lesson: scalar linear systems can be solved with matrix-valued unknowns when all unknowns have the same fixed shape.

Tutorial 3 — Construct a transformation from basis images

A linear map T sends (1,0)T to (2,−1,0)T and (0,1)T to (1,3,4)T. Find its standard matrix and T(3,−2).

Solution. Place the two output vectors in columns, not rows. The matrix is A = [21−1304], of shape 3-by-2. The input equals 3e1−2e2, so linearity yields three times the first column minus twice the second. This is (4,−9,−8)T. Row-column evaluation confirms the entries: 6−2, −3−6, and 0−8.

A two-by-three arrangement of the given images would act on three-dimensional inputs and could not represent this map. Lesson: the number of columns is the input dimension; the number of rows is the output dimension. Basis images completely determine a linear map once the input basis is fixed.

Tutorial 4 — One product, four calculations

For A = [1−12031] and B = [2014−12], compute AB and verify the second row and first column through the row and column views.

Solution. The output is 2-by-2. Its four row-column sums are 2−1−2 = −1, 0−4+4 = 0, 0+3−1 = 2, and 0+12+2 = 14. Thus AB = [−10214]. The second row of A is (0,3,1), so the second output row is zero times row 1 of B, plus three times row 2, plus row 3: (3,12)+(−1,2) = (2,14). The first column of B supplies coefficients (2,1,−1); combining A's columns gives (2,0)+(−1,3)+(−2,−1) = (−1,2).

The outer-product terms are [2000], [−1−4312], and [−24−12]. Their sum confirms every output entry. Lesson: select the view that exposes sparsity or structure; all four views compute the same product.

Tutorial 5 — Distributivity with a complete verification

Course-derived type: MIT 18.06SC multiplication recitation, Problem 3.1. The numerical data and explanation here are new. Let A = [2−113], B = [1000], and C = [004−2]. Verify A(B+C) = AB+AC and explain why this example alone is not a universal proof.

Solution. B+C = [104−2]. Multiplying gives A(B+C) = [−2213−6]. Separately, AB = [2010] and AC = [−4212−6]; their sum is the same matrix. Each output entry has split the two contributions into separate sums.

The calculation establishes the identity for these particular matrices. The general identity requires the arbitrary-entry argument from Section 5, where distributivity of scalar multiplication is applied inside the shared-index sum. Lesson: an example illustrates a theorem; arbitrary-entry reasoning proves its universal scope.

Tutorial 6 — Quantities, prices, and physical units

Course-derived type: CMU 21-241 Day 7 quantities-times-prices application. A laboratory buys three consumable types. Two teams request Q = [325142] units, with teams as rows and consumables as columns. Two suppliers charge P = [235412] dollars per unit, with consumables as rows and suppliers as columns. Compute the total costs and select the cheaper supplier for each team.

Solution. QP is 2-by-2: team-by-supplier. The first team's costs are 3·2+2·5+5·1 = 21 and 3·3+2·4+5·2 = 27. The second team's costs are 1·2+4·5+2·1 = 24 and 1·3+4·4+2·2 = 23. Thus QP = [21272423]. Team one chooses supplier one; team two chooses supplier two.

Every term has units of units purchased times dollars per unit, so the result is dollars. Multiplying corresponding entries would be undefined as a same-shape operation and would not sum over consumables. Lesson: semantic row and column labels can be as useful as numerical dimensions when modeling a problem.

Tutorial 7 — Select rows, columns, and one entry

Let A = [7−25140]. Compute Ae2, e2TA, and e1TAe3. Specify every selector's dimension.

Solution. On the right, e2 is the three-coordinate vector (0,1,0)T, so Ae2 = (−2,4)T, the second column. On the left, e2 is the two-coordinate vector (0,1)T, so e2TA = (1,4,0), the second row. The final left selector has two coordinates, the right selector three; their product extracts entry (1,3), equal to five.

The same notation e2 has different ambient dimensions in different positions. That is legitimate when the context fixes the dimensions, but omitting this distinction in a proof can make an expression invalid. Lesson: coordinate selectors are shape-dependent objects.

Tutorial 8 — Compose two outer-product maps

Let u,w be real m-coordinate columns and v,z real m-coordinate columns. Find (uvT)(wzT) and characterize when it vanishes if u and z are nonzero.

Solution. Associate the middle factors: the product equals u(vTw)zT. Since vTw is a scalar, this equals (vTw)uzT. When u and z are nonzero, their outer product is nonzero: choose nonzero coordinates ui and zj, and their product is a nonzero entry. Thus the matrix product vanishes exactly when vTw = 0.

Take u = z = (1,0)T, v = (0,1)T, and w = (1,0)T. Both outer-product matrices are nonzero, but their product is zero because the first map reads a coordinate that the second map's output does not contain. Lesson: zero products can reflect orthogonality of an internal scalar pairing, not zero factors.

Tutorial 9 — Reverse a shear and a rotation

Use S = [1101] and R = [0−110]. Compute RS, SR, and both products on x = (1,1)T.

Solution. RS = [0−111] while SR = [1−110]. Applying RS to x gives (−1,2)T. Applying SR gives (0,1)T. To understand the first answer, shear x to (2,1), then rotate it to (−1,2). For the second, rotate x to (−1,1), then shear it to (0,1).

The commutator RS−SR = [−1001] is nonzero and sends x to (−1,1), exactly the difference of the two outputs. Lesson: follow the action sequence on a vector before choosing the written matrix order; the rightmost factor acts first.

Tutorial 10 — Nonzero factors, zero product, and failed cancellation

Let D = [1000], B = [0010], and C = 0. Show that DB = DC although B ≠ C. Explain exactly what information D loses.

Solution. Every column of B has zero first coordinate. D keeps a vector's first coordinate and sets its second to zero, so it kills every column of B. Thus DB = 0 = DC. Yet B has a one in its lower-left position and is not C. Premultiplication by D discards the entire second row of any matrix. Equality after applying D therefore cannot recover that discarded row.

No contradiction with cancellation for invertible matrices exists: D has no inverse, since D(0,1)T = 0. Merely being nonzero is not a cancellation hypothesis. Lesson: translate A(B−C) = 0 into a statement about each difference column before drawing conclusions.

Tutorial 11 — Equality on a basis versus one vector

Suppose A and B are m-by-n. Prove that Aej = Bej for every standard basis vector implies A = B. Give different two-by-two matrices that agree on (1,0)T.

Solution. Multiplication by ej extracts column j. The hypothesis therefore says every corresponding pair of columns agrees. Entrywise equality follows for every row and column, proving A = B. Choose A = I and B = [1403]. Their first columns both equal (1,0)T, so they agree on the specified vector, but their second columns differ.

More generally, equality on any basis is enough because every input is a linear combination of basis vectors and the maps are linear. Equality on a set that does not span the input space can leave unconstrained directions. Lesson: the quantifier “for every input” or “for every basis vector” carries essential information.

Tutorial 12 — Rectangular left and right inverses

Let A = [100100] and L = [100010]. Compute LA and AL. Explain which cancellation direction A permits and why A is not invertible in the square-matrix sense.

Solution. LA = I2, but AL = diag(1,1,0), not I3. The map A embeds a two-coordinate vector into three coordinates by appending zero, and L reads the first two coordinates. Therefore L undoes A on every input. However, applying L to (0,0,1)T loses its third coordinate and A cannot restore it.

If AX = AY, premultiply by L to obtain X = Y. A therefore permits left cancellation in this form. It has a left inverse but cannot have a two-sided inverse of the definition in Section 7 because it is rectangular. Lesson: one-sided inverse equations must retain the identity dimensions; LA = I does not imply AL = I for rectangular pairs.

Tutorial 13 — Solve an equation with factors on both sides

Let A = [1101], B = diag(2,3), and C = [4623]. Solve AXB = C and verify the solution.

Solution. Undo A on the left and B on the right. Their inverses are A−1 = [1−101] and B−1 = diag(1/2,1/3). First A−1C = [2323]. Right multiplication by B−1 scales the first column by one half and the second by one third, so X = [1111]. Verification gives AX = [2211], followed by AXB = [4623].

The tempting expression B−1CA−1 uses the wrong sides and generally solves a different problem. Lesson: erase factors by multiplying inverses next to the factor being erased, and preserve all other order.

Tutorial 14 — Transpose a rectangular product

Let A = [120−134] and B = [21−1]. Compute (AB)T directly and through the product rule.

Solution. AB is a two-coordinate column: its entries are 2+2+0 = 4 and −2+3−4 = −3. Thus (AB)T is the row (4,−3). The rule gives BTAT, a one-by-three matrix times a three-by-two matrix. Its first entry is 2·1+1·2+(−1)·0 = 4; its second is 2·(−1)+1·3+(−1)·4 = −3.

The incorrect order ATBT would be three-by-two times one-by-three and is not even defined. Lesson: rectangular examples reveal order errors that square dimensions might conceal.

Tutorial 15 — Distinguish transpose from adjoint

Let z = (1,i)T and A = [1i21−i]. Find zTz, z∗z, AT, and A∗.

Solution. Ordinary transpose gives zTz = 1+i2 = 0. Conjugate transpose gives z∗z = 1+(−i)i = 2. The transpose is [12i1−i]. The adjoint is [12−i1+i]. Both swap rows and columns; only the adjoint conjugates entries.

The squared Euclidean length is two, not zero. Ordinary matrix multiplication remains bilinear and does not insert a conjugate, while the complex inner product does. Lesson: a nonzero complex vector can have zero bilinear self-product without having zero norm.

Tutorial 16 — Symmetric/skew decomposition and its uniqueness

Decompose A = [25−14] into symmetric H and skew-symmetric K. Evaluate xTAx for x = (1,2)T through H and explain why K contributes nothing.

Solution. AT = [2−154]. The half-sum gives H = [2224]; the half-difference gives K = [03−30]. Their sum is A. Hx = (6,10)T, so xTHx = 6+20 = 26. Kx = (6,−3)T, and xTKx = 6−6 = 0. Directly Ax = (12,7)T, giving 12+14 = 26.

If another decomposition existed, its symmetric difference would equal a skew-symmetric difference. Transposing would show that difference equals its own negative, hence is zero. Lesson: the decomposition is unique, and a real quadratic expression sees only its symmetric component.

Tutorial 17 — Symmetric factors do not ensure a symmetric product

Let A = diag(1,2) and B = [0110]. Are A, B, and AB symmetric? Prove the condition for a product of two symmetric matrices to be symmetric.

Solution. Both A and B equal their transposes. Their product is [0120], which is not symmetric because its off-diagonal entries differ. The reversed product is [0210], exactly the transpose of AB.

For any symmetric A and B of the same size, (AB)T = BTAT = BA. Thus AB is symmetric if and only if AB = BA. This establishes both necessity and sufficiency. Lesson: closure under addition does not imply closure under multiplication; a structural condition can impose a commutation requirement.

Tutorial 18 — Gram matrix, negative entries, and strict positivity

Let A = [1−10210]. Find ATA, verify its quadratic value directly, and decide whether it is positive definite.

Solution. The columns are (1,0,1)T and (−1,2,0)T, with squared lengths two and five and mutual dot product −1. Hence G = [2−1−15]. For x = (u,v)T, Ax = (u−v,2v,u)T, giving xTGx = (u−v)2+4v2+u2 = 2u2−2uv+5v2.

This sum of squares vanishes only when u = 0 and v = 0, so the matrix is positive definite. Its negative off-diagonal entries do not conflict with positivity: positivity refers to the quadratic value for every nonzero vector. Lesson: prove a Gram claim by expressing the quadratic value as a squared norm.

Tutorial 19 — Rectangular orthonormal columns

Let Q = [100001]. Compute QTQ and QQT. Does Q preserve lengths? Does it preserve every three-dimensional vector after QT followed by Q?

Solution. The two columns are perpendicular unit vectors, so QTQ = I2. The reverse product is diag(1,0,1). For input (a,b)T, Q outputs (a,0,b)T, preserving squared length a2+b2. On a three-dimensional vector (r,s,t)T, QQT returns (r,0,t)T and discards the middle coordinate.

Thus Q is a length-preserving embedding, while QQT is a projection onto its column plane. It is not the three-dimensional identity. Lesson: orthonormal columns imply input-length preservation but not a two-sided identity unless the matrix is square.

Tutorial 20 — Two-by-two inverse and a singular parameter

For A(t) = [1t23], find the inverse when it exists. Exhibit a nonzero vector killed by A when it does not exist.

Solution. The denominator from direct multiplication is 3−2t. For t ≠ 3/2, the inverse is 13−2t[3−t−21]. Multiplying the numerator matrix on either side of A yields (3−2t)I, which verifies the formula.

At t = 3/2 the vector (−3,2)T is nonzero and is mapped to (−3+3,−6+6)T = 0. An inverse would have to recover this vector from zero, impossible for a linear map. Lesson: identify exceptional parameter values before dividing; check both the existence condition and the claimed inverse.

Tutorial 21 — Inverse of a product: reverse the order

Let A = [1101] and B = diag(2,3). Compute (AB)−1, and show A−1B−1 is incorrect.

Solution. AB = [2303]. The correct inverse B−1A−1 is [12−12013]. Multiplication by AB gives diagonal entries one and off-diagonal entry 2·(−1/2)+3·(1/3) = 0. The opposite-side check also gives I.

The wrong order yields [12−13013]. Multiplying AB by it gives top-right entry −2/3+1 = 1/3, so the product is not I. Lesson: transpose and inverse both reverse product order, for different but compatible algebraic reasons.

Tutorial 22 — Diagonal scaling and a permutation cycle

For A = [123456789], D = diag(2,−1,3), and P = [001100010], describe DA, AD, PA, and AP.

Solution. DA scales rows: [246−4−5−6212427]. AD scales columns: [2−298−51814−827]. The columns of P are e2, e3, e1, so AP has A's columns 2,3,1, giving [231564897]. On the left, P selects A's rows 3,1,2, giving [789123456].

The row and column permutation orders differ because they are determined by P's rows and columns, respectively. PT is its inverse and P3 = I, but P2 is not I. Lesson: a permutation matrix need not be a simple self-inverse swap.

Tutorial 23 — Square expansion and a false difference of squares

Let A = [1101] and B = diag(1,2). Compare (A+B)2 with A2+2AB+B2, and derive the correct expansion of (A−B)(A+B).

Solution. AB = [1202] and BA = [1102]. Their difference is [0100]. The correct square expansion is A2+AB+BA+B2. Replacing BA with AB changes the answer by AB−BA. Directly A+B = [2103], whose square is [4509]. The false scalar-style formula gives [4609].

Distributing the other product gives (A−B)(A+B) = A2+AB−BA−B2. It equals A2−B2 exactly when AB = BA. Lesson: distribute first, preserving order, and only combine cross terms after establishing commutation.

Tutorial 24 — A nilpotent three-by-three inverse

Course-derived type: MIT 18.06SC recitation Problem 3.2, also identified there as Strang, Section 2.5, Problem 24. Derive the upper-triangular inverse by multiplication rather than Gaussian elimination. Let U = [1ab01c001].

Solution. Write U = I+N, where N has entries a,b,c above the diagonal and zeros elsewhere. Direct multiplication gives N2 = [00ac000000], while N3 = 0. The alternating finite series therefore gives U−1 = I−N+N2 = [1−aac−b01−c001].

Check the top-right product entry: (ac−b)+a(−c)+b = 0. The adjacent upper entries also cancel, and all diagonal entries equal one. In the reverse product the top-right entry is b−ac+(ac−b) = 0. Both sides give I. Lesson: the ac term records a two-step path through the middle coordinate; simply negating all off-diagonal entries misses that interaction.

Tutorial 25 — Powers of an idempotent matrix

Let P = 15[1224]. Prove P2 = P. For positive integer k, derive (I+P)k without diagonalization.

Solution. Squaring the numerator matrix gives [5101020], equal to five times that numerator. Including the factor 1/25 gives P again. Every positive power of P is consequently P. Since I commutes with P, the binomial theorem applies. Its constant term is I, and the coefficient multiplying P is the sum of all nonconstant binomial coefficients, 2k−1. Thus (I+P)k = I+(2k−1)P.

An alternative proof applies induction and uses P2 = P at the multiplication step. Lesson: a low-degree polynomial relation can determine all higher powers; eigenvalue theory is not always necessary.

Tutorial 26 — A nonzero matrix with no square root

Course-derived type: Oxford M1, printed p. 13, Example 29. Prove that N = [0100] has no two-by-two square root over ℝ or ℂ.

Solution. Suppose X = [abcd] satisfies X2 = N. Entrywise, a2+bc = 0, b(a+d) = 1, c(a+d) = 0, and d2+bc = 0. The second equation forces a+d ≠ 0 and b ≠ 0. The third therefore forces c = 0. The first now yields a2 = 0 and hence a = 0; the fourth yields d = 0. But then b(a+d) = 0, contradicting its required value one.

The argument works over the real and complex fields because a scalar with square zero is zero in either field. Lesson: existence of matrix powers does not imply existence of matrix roots. Scalar intuitions about square roots cannot be imported automatically.

Tutorial 27 — Block dimensions and a triangular block inverse

Let X be 2-by-3. Form M = [I2X0I3]. State M's size, derive its inverse, and explain why the lower-left zero block is 3-by-2.

Solution. The row block sizes are two and three, and the column block sizes are two and three, so M is 5-by-5. The lower-left block must have three rows and two columns. Try N = [I2−X0I3]. Multiplying compatible blocks gives top-left I2, bottom-right I3, lower-left zero, and top-right −X+X = 0. The reverse product has the same cancellation. Thus N is M's inverse.

The fact that X is rectangular causes no problem: the off-diagonal products are I2X and XI3, both 2-by-3. Lesson: identities and zeros in a block expression may have different shapes; write them from the row and column partitions.

Tutorial 28 — A block commutator

For square X and Y of the same size, let M = [IX0I] and N = [I0YI]. Compute MN and NM. When do they commute?

Solution. Block multiplication gives MN = [I+XYXYI] and NM = [IXYI+YX]. Their off-diagonal blocks agree. The top-left blocks agree exactly when XY = 0, and the bottom-right blocks agree exactly when YX = 0. Both conditions are necessary and together sufficient.

A claim that they commute whenever XY = YX would be false: taking X = Y = I makes the products unequal. A claim that XY = 0 alone suffices is also false for general matrices because YX may remain nonzero. Lesson: compare every block of the entire expression; equality of one internal product is not automatically equality of two larger block matrices.

Tutorial 29 — Prove and use triangular closure

Let A = [21403−2005] and B = [1200−13002]. Compute their diagonal product entries without full multiplication and prove the product is upper triangular.

Solution. On a diagonal entry (i,i), a nonzero term requires i ≤ k from A and k ≤ i from B, so k = i is the only contributor. The diagonal of AB is therefore (2,−3,10). Below the diagonal, i > j, a nonzero contribution would require i ≤ k ≤ j, which is impossible; every term is zero.

If desired, the full product is [23110−350010]: the top-right is 0+3+8 = 11 and the middle-right 9−4 = 5. Lesson: prove zero structure first; it can eliminate most arithmetic and expose impossible proposed answers immediately.

Tutorial 30 — Trace of rectangular products

Let A = [1200−13] and B = [2014−21]. Compute AB, the diagonal of BA, and both traces. Does trace equality imply product equality?

Solution. AB = [48−7−1], with trace three. BA is three-by-three; its diagonal entries come from row 1 of B paired with column 1 of A, row 2 paired with column 2, and row 3 paired with column 3. They are two, −2, and three, respectively, again summing to three. The shapes of the products differ, so the matrices cannot be equal.

The general equality follows by interchanging the two finite sums in the trace expansion, not by commuting the matrices. Lesson: a trace identity is a scalar equality; it must not be promoted to an equality of matrices.

Tutorial 31 — Cyclic trace is not arbitrary swapping

Use square matrix units A = E12, B = E21, C = E11 in dimension two. Find tr(ABC), tr(BCA), and tr(ACB).

Solution. The unit rule gives AB = E11, so ABC = E11 and its trace is one. BC = E21, followed by A on the right, gives BCA = E22, also trace one. In contrast AC = E12E11 = 0 because the middle indices do not match. Thus ACB = 0 and its trace is zero.

BCA is a cyclic rotation of ABC. ACB exchanges only the final two factors and is not such a rotation. Lesson: trace can rotate the full factor order; it cannot erase noncommutativity.

Tutorial 32 — Frobenius norm and decomposition geometry

For A = [25−14], compute the Frobenius norms of A, its symmetric part H, and its skew part K from Problem 16. Verify the squared norm decomposition.

Solution. The squared norm of A is 4+25+1+16 = 46. For H = [2224], it is 4+4+4+16 = 28. For K = [03−30], it is 0+9+9+0 = 18. Hence 46 = 28+18. Their Frobenius inner product is 2·0+2·3+2·(−3)+4·0 = 0, which explains the Pythagorean relation.

The squared norms add, not the norms themselves. Also this is a matrix-entry geometry statement, distinct from whether A preserves vector lengths. Lesson: write the norm's subscript and square explicitly; several different norms and geometries coexist in linear algebra.

Tutorial 33 — Two nonstandard products

For A = [1203] and B = [40−12], compute A ⊙ B, AB, and A ⊗ B. State their shapes.

Solution. The Hadamard product is [4006], obtained by corresponding-entry multiplication. Ordinary multiplication gives [24−36], because each output entry sums two intermediate products. Both are 2-by-2 but differ. The Kronecker product is [4080−12−240012000−36], of shape 4-by-4, consisting of blocks B, 2B, zero, and 3B.

The three products answer different mathematical questions. Identical shapes do not make the first two operations interchangeable, and the third deliberately enlarges the dimension. Lesson: determine the product symbol before applying a rule.

Tutorial 34 — Exact operation counts and parenthesization

For A of shape 10-by-100, B 100-by-5, and C 5-by-50, compare both parenthesizations using classical multiplication. Count multiplications and minimal additions separately.

Solution. AB costs 10·100·5 = 5,000 multiplications and 10·5·99 = 4,950 additions. Then (AB)C costs 10·5·50 = 2,500 multiplications and 10·50·4 = 2,000 additions. Totals are 7,500 and 6,950.

For the other route, BC costs 100·5·50 = 25,000 multiplications and 100·50·4 = 20,000 additions. A(BC) costs 10·100·50 = 50,000 multiplications and 10·50·99 = 49,500 additions. Totals are 75,000 and 69,500. Both routes produce a 10-by-50 matrix. Lesson: associativity allows a tenfold reduction in this example's classical scalar counts, without changing the factor order or exact result.

Tutorial 35 — A graph power counts walks

Let G = [010101010], the adjacency matrix of an undirected three-vertex path. Compute G2 and explain the meaning of its diagonal and off-diagonal entries. Prove the walk-count interpretation for all nonnegative integer powers.

Solution. Multiplication gives G2 = [101020101]. Entry (1,3) is one because the sole two-edge walk is 1→2→3. Entry (2,2) is two because 2→1→2 and 2→3→2 both return to vertex two. These are walks; revisiting a vertex is allowed, so the diagonal is not necessarily zero.

For zero steps, I counts one empty walk from each vertex to itself. Inductively, (Gk+1)ij sums (Gk)irGrj over the penultimate vertex r. Every length-(k+1) walk has exactly one such vertex and one final edge, so the sum counts each walk exactly once. Lesson: powers encode repeated composition; distinguish walks from simple paths.

Tutorial 36 — Perturbation identity and an explicit bound

Let A = diag(2,1), B = I, E = [0ε00], and F = [00ε0], with real ε. Compute the exact product error and compare its Frobenius norm to the general bound.

Solution. AF = [00ε0], EB = [0ε00], and EF = [ε2000]. Thus (A+E)(B+F)−AB = [ε2εε0]. Its squared Frobenius norm is ε4+2ε2, giving norm |ε|√(ε2+2).

The general bound gives √5|ε|+√2|ε|+ε2 because ‖A‖F = √5, ‖B‖F = √2, and both perturbation norms equal |ε|. This bound is valid but conservative. Omitting EF gives a first-order approximation whose neglected norm is ε2; it is not the exact product. Lesson: retain the mixed perturbation term in an identity and state explicitly when you make an approximation.

Mathematical constructions needed by the examination bank

The full matrix-algebra lesson above establishes shapes, composition, transposes, inverse identities, blocks and computational counts. The bank also uses elementary determinant, dimension and coordinate arguments. The following constructions teach the exact additional results used here. Full elimination, general spectral theory and numerical factorization retain their later chapters. The four freshly rechecked core university texts supply the algebraic foundations; these proof expansions are independently written and are not attributed to unread course sections.

1. Determinant means an alternating volume function, not a diagonal shortcut

For a square matrix of positive size, define

detA=∑π∈Snsgn(π)∏i=1nai,π(i).

The sum ranges over permutations, so every product chooses one entry from each row and each column. For a two-by-two matrix this gives a11a22−a12a21. The off-diagonal term is part of the definition. A general three-by-three matrix likewise involves six signed products; it cannot automatically use three diagonal entries alone.

The formula is linear in each column while the others are fixed. Swapping two columns changes the sign because it reindexes permutations with an odd swap. If two columns coincide, exchanging them leaves the array unchanged but negates its determinant, so the determinant is zero over the real or complex field. These facts prove the normalized alternating multilinear property, with detIn=1.

They also prove multiplicativity without assuming commutation. Write each column of AB as a combination of columns of A, with coefficients supplied by the corresponding column of B. Multilinearly expand the determinant. Any term selecting one A column twice vanishes. The surviving choices select all n columns in a permutation order. The determinant of each such ordered selection is its permutation sign times detA. Summing its scalar coefficients gives exactly the permutation formula for detB. Therefore det(AB)=detAdetB. Only scalar coefficients were rearranged; no matrix factors were commuted.

If A is upper triangular, a nonzero permutation term requires π(i)≥i for every i. Summing these inequalities and using ∑iπ(i)=∑ii forces equality for every index. Only the identity permutation survives, giving detA=∏iaii. This is a sufficient structural guarantee. A nontriangular matrix can coincidentally have the same determinant and diagonal product; that does not extend the shortcut to arbitrary matrices.

Multiplicativity implies similarity invariance: for invertible B, the identity B−1B=I gives det(B−1)=1/detB, and hence det(B−1AB)=detA. Row multilinearity gives det(cA)=cndetA, while trace scales only by c. These two scalar summaries measure different aspects of a transformation.

2. Constraints must be counted by independent functionals

Let L:V→W be a linear map on a finite-dimensional domain. Choose a basis k1,…,kr of its kernel and extend it to a basis k1,…,kr,v1,…,vs of V. Every image is a combination of L(vj) because the kernel contributions vanish. If ∑jcjL(vj)=0, then ∑jcjvj is a kernel vector and therefore a combination of the ki. Independence of the extended basis forces every cj=0. Thus L(v1),…,L(vs) form a basis of the image and

dimV=dimkerL+dimimL.

On symmetric n×n matrices, the independent coordinates are the n diagonal entries and (n2) upper off-diagonal entries. Mirrored lower cells are determined values. Trace is a nonzero functional: applying it to E11 gives one. Trace zero therefore removes exactly one dimension. Adding a specified off-diagonal zero removes a second dimension when that coordinate exists, because evaluating the two proposed functionals on E11 and Eij+Eji proves their independence. Repeating the reflected equation does not remove a third dimension.

This theorem classifies real linear degrees of freedom. It does not count integer solutions. The authentic coupled nonnegative equations first require a reversible subtraction, then enumeration of lattice points in disjoint variable groups. Their affine dimension is three; their integer cardinality is 336. A correct matrix-rank statement can be an incorrect answer to a different counting question.

3. A rank bound becomes an equality only after information loss is excluded

For compatible maps V then U, the product image is U(imV). Its dimension cannot exceed either the intermediate image dimension or the total image dimension of U. This proves the familiar upper bound. It does not prove equality, since U may kill part of imV.

For the bank's n×2 full-column-rank U and 2×n full-row-rank V, the first action V reaches every two-coordinate vector, and the second U loses none of those vectors. Hence the product image is exactly imU and its rank is two. Injectivity also proves ker(UV)=kerV. The hypotheses require n≥2; at n=2 the product is invertible, while at larger sizes it has nullity n−2.

The reverse action order can behave very differently. At n=5, take U=[e1e2] and let V read the third and fourth coordinates. The product UV maps (x1,x2,x3,x4,x5) to (x3,x4,0,0,0). It has rank two and square zero. In contrast VU=0. Both factors have their maximum possible rank, yet they are neither square inverses nor a guarantee of full rank in the reverse product. This is a concrete composition explanation, not a contradiction of the rank bound.

4. Nilpotent powers record chronological paths

For the three-coordinate shift, N moves coordinate three to two and two to one. Two moves reach coordinate one, and three moves are impossible. Thus N2=E13 and N3=0. Expanding (I+N)k is justified because its two summands commute. A term that contributes to the upper-right entry selects N at two distinct time slots, with identity at all other slots. There are (k2) choices. One slot cannot perform both moves.

For weights a,b,c above the diagonal,

N=(0ab00c000),(I+N)13k=kb+k(k−1)2ac.

The first term is a direct move; the second passes through the middle coordinate. At nonnegative integer powers zero and one, the indirect contribution vanishes. At negative integer powers, derive the inverse I−N+N2 first. The polynomial identity I+kN+k(k−1)N2/2 continues to satisfy the integer group law because N3=0, but the negative coefficient expression is a falling-factorial polynomial, not an ordinary count of choosing a negative number of slots.

For a strictly upper-triangular matrix of size n, any potentially nonzero product entry of Nk follows a strictly increasing index chain of k edges. No chain of n edges exists among n indices, so Nn=0. The actual Oxford definition correctly includes zero diagonal entries; this proof is an instructional expansion, not a correction of that definition.

5. Coordinate conversion has three separately justified stages

Let B contain the new input basis vectors in standard coordinates. A coordinate list c represents the physical vector Bc. A standard matrix T maps that vector to TBc. If the same new basis is used on output, the output list is B−1TBc, and the new array is B−1TB. Each column can be checked by transforming one basis vector and solving for its coefficients.

For different input and output bases, with matrices B,C, the array is C−1TB. Calling this a similarity would be incorrect unless the same ordered basis is used on both sides. Trace and determinant invariance concern similarity, not arbitrary independent coordinate changes. A rectangular transformation has separate input and output spaces and naturally uses two basis matrices.

For B=(111−1) and T=diag(2,n), the second output image is (2,−n). The equations c1+c2=2 and c1−c2=−n give coefficients (2−n)/2 and (2+n)/2. This explicit coefficient solution explains the off-diagonal value and the common half-factor error before any compact conjugation formula is memorized.

6. Block inverse construction undoes the diagonal actions and their coupling

For compatible block coordinates (x,y), the matrix (AC0D) sends them to (Ax+Cy,Dy). If A,D are invertible, solve backward: first y=D−1v, then x=A−1u−A−1CD−1v. Therefore

(AC0D)−1=(A−1−A−1CD−10D−1).

The coupling block can be rectangular or singular. Its inverse is never required. Both ordered products verify the formula, while changing factor order in its upper-right block generally fails. With identity diagonal blocks, the inverse coupling is simply negative C. With A=I,D=2I, it is −C/2 because the lower output must first be divided by two.

Two opposing block shears need not commute. Their products have diagonal blocks I+XY,I in one order and I,I+YX in the other. Equality requires both XY=0 and YX=0, not just XY=YX. Taking X=Y=I gives equal internal products but unequal full block matrices. A new lower-left coupling also removes the automatic block-triangular determinant shortcut.

7. The Gram kernel theorem uses positivity and a declared field

For real A, the implication Ax=0⇒ATAx=0 is immediate. For the reverse implication, the identity xTATAx=∑i(Ax)i2 turns zero into a sum of nonnegative real terms. Every term must vanish. Thus the two kernels agree and rank–nullity makes their ranks agree.

For complex matrices the proof requires A* and squared absolute values. The column (1,i)T has ordinary bilinear self-product zero but Hermitian squared length two. Therefore using transpose in an unlabeled complex positivity argument is not a harmless typographical choice. Similarly, a positive-semidefinite weight can kill a nonzero output; a positive-definite weight is needed for ker(A*HA)=kerA without extra restrictions.

Positive definiteness of the equicorrelation matrix is proved by decomposing the full space into the all-equal line and its sum-zero complement. For dimension d≥2, the two coefficients are 1+(d−1)a and 1−a. Both must be strictly positive. Their positivity is sufficient because the decomposition exhausts every vector; testing a few random coordinates alone would not establish the theorem.

Formula and conceptual problem bank

This bank combines authentic Iranian entrance-examination questions, newly authored medium/hard analogues, and two retained multistep challenges. The original four-option numbering is retained for authentic questions. Difficulty labels for original problems are qualitative author judgments, not calibrated response statistics.

Authentic examinations · Original analogues · Integrated challenges

Authentic examination questions

The coupled integer-equation item is a cross-topic boundary example: real linear-system dimension alone does not count nonnegative integer solutions.

Question 1. MSc CS 1405, Q41 — Dimension with simultaneous constraints

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 9 · question 41. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

Let W be the real vector space of symmetric 4×4 matrices with trace zero. What is dimW?

1.

10

2.

9

3.

8

4.

7

Read the complete derivation, checks, and diagnosed alternatives

Correct option: 2.

Model the independent coordinates explicitly

A real symmetric four-by-four matrix has the form

S=(d1abcad2efbed3gcfgd4).

The six off-diagonal coordinates a,b,c,e,f,g are unconstrained; symmetry means each is copied into a second entry, not independently chosen twice. Trace zero means d1+d2+d3+d4=0, so d4=−d1−d2−d3. Thus all admissible matrices are uniquely described by nine real parameters: six off-diagonal entries and three diagonal entries. This unique parameterization proves dimension nine.

A concrete basis is Eij+Eji for 1≤i<j≤4, together with E11−E44,E22−E44,E33−E44. Every element is symmetric and trace zero. A zero linear combination forces the six off-diagonal coefficients to vanish by inspecting their entries, and then forces the three remaining coefficients to vanish by inspecting the first three diagonal entries. The nine matrices are therefore independent and span the space.

Option 1's ten ignores the trace restriction. Options 3 and 4 remove two or three dimensions instead of the rank-one constraint. Trace zero does not mean zero diagonal: diag(1,−1,0,0) is a valid nonzero diagonal element. The trace functional has rank one because it takes value one on E11; writing equivalent copies of its equation does not create extra rank.

For positive size n, the corresponding real dimension is n(n+1)/2−1. At n=1 the space contains only zero and has dimension zero. At n=0, trace is already zero on the zero-dimensional space, so a separate dimension-zero answer is required; subtracting one would be invalid.

Exact verification ledger

Parameter family Independent count Why
Off-diagonal symmetric pairs 6 Upper and lower entries are linked.
Trace-zero diagonal entries 3 The fourth cancels the other three.
Total 9 The two families form an independent basis.

Question 2. MSc CS 1405, Q113 — Coupled nonnegative equations

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 25 · question 113. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

How many nonnegative integer solutions satisfy x1+x2+x3=5 and x1+x2+x3+x4+x5=20?

1.

37

2.
(244)+(72)
3.
(244)(72)
4.

336

Read the complete derivation, checks, and diagnosed alternatives

Correct option: 4. The number is 336. The original PDF's first alternative is 37, correcting an earlier transcription as 32.

Remove the coupled sum before counting

Subtract the first equation from the second. This is a reversible operation on the two constraints and gives

x1+x2+x3=5,x4+x5=15.

The variable groups are now disjoint. For a fixed x1=t, the pairs (x2,x3) are (0,5−t),(1,4−t),…,(5−t,0), exactly 6−t choices. Sum over t=0,…,5:

6+5+4+3+2+1=21=(72).

For the second group choose x4=s with s=0,…,15; then x5=15−s is forced. These are sixteen choices, including both zero endpoints. Every first-group triple can be paired with every second-group pair, and every admissible five-tuple has exactly one such decomposition. This bijection proves the product, rather than an unsupported assumption of independent equations:

21·16=336.
Alternative Exact value Why it fails
Add the two group counts 21+16=37 This counts choosing one group or the other, instead of supplying both.
Add unrestricted five-variable count (244)+21=10647 The unrestricted total-sum equation does not enforce the first-group sum.
Multiply that unrestricted count (244)·21=223146 Each counted object carries an extra choice; it is not one uniquely admissible tuple.
Product of the two disjoint-group counts 336 Every allowed tuple is counted once.

Why matrix rank does not answer this question

Over the reals, the coefficient rows are independent and the affine solution set has dimension 5−2=3. That describes continuous degrees of freedom; it is not the cardinality of its nonnegative integer points. The nonnegative boundaries make a finite lattice problem. For totals r and t, the same decomposition gives (r+22)(t−r+1) when 0≤r≤t are integers, and zero if t<r. These domain tests must precede the counting formula. No official answer key is invented: option 4 is independently derived from the original statement.

Question 3. PhD CS 1404, Q30 — A lower norm bound does not imply positivity

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 8 · question 30. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

A real square matrix A satisfies ‖Ax‖≥θ‖x‖ for every real x, with θ>0. Which assertion is false?

1.

‖A−1‖≤θ−1 for the induced norm.

2.

A is positive definite.

3.

A is nonsingular.

4.

If λ is an eigenvalue of A, then |λ|≥θ.

Read the complete derivation, checks, and diagnosed alternatives

Correct option: 2.

The hypothesis controls magnitude, not the sign of a quadratic form. Take A=−I and θ=1. For every vector and every norm, ‖Ax‖=‖−x‖=‖x‖. Yet for every nonzero real x, xTAx=−‖x‖22<0. Thus positive definiteness does not follow, and option 2 is the false general assertion.

To check option 3, suppose Ax=0. The bound gives 0≥θ‖x‖, and θ>0 forces x=0. A square real matrix with a trivial kernel is invertible. This uses squareness: a tall injective rectangular map need not have a two-sided inverse.

For option 1, put x=A−1y in the original inequality. Then ‖y‖≥θ‖A−1y‖. Dividing by θ‖y‖ for y≠0 and taking the supremum yields the corresponding induced operator norm bound

‖A−1‖≤θ−1.

For a real eigenvalue with real eigenvector v≠0, substituting Av=λv directly gives |λ|≥θ. Nonreal eigenvalues need an additional argument because the original vectors are real. With the Euclidean norm, write a complex eigenvector v=u+iw and apply the squared real bound to u and w separately. Adding gives ‖Av‖22≥θ2‖v‖22, hence the same modulus bound.

The conclusion also holds for any finite-dimensional real norm with its induced matrix norm. Set B=A−1; then ‖Bk‖≤θ−k. Norm equivalence gives constants c,C>0 with c‖x‖2≤‖x‖≤C‖x‖2 on real vectors. Therefore ‖Bkx‖2≤(C/c)θ−k‖x‖2. Extend this upper Euclidean bound to complex vectors by summing the bounds for real and imaginary parts. For an eigenvalue μ of B, it gives |μ|k≤(C/c)θ−k. Taking k th roots and letting k grow gives |μ|≤θ−1, so the eigenvalue λ=1/μ of A has |λ|≥θ. This justifies option 4 without silently imposing a Euclidean norm on the source's unqualified notation.

Finite-dimensional norm equivalence here follows by bounding a norm on the Euclidean unit sphere: continuity follows from the triangle inequality and coordinate expansion, the compact sphere has a finite maximum, and its minimum is positive because a norm vanishes only at zero. The complex argument is an extension of a real norm bound, not an assertion that the original real norm is automatically a complex inner product.

Question 4. PhD CS 1404, Q31 — Orthogonal projection and a reversed inequality

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 8 · question 31. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

An orthogonal basis u1,…,un spans U⊆ℝm, with n≤m. Let Px=∑k=1n⟨x,uk⟩uk. Which statement is false?

Original-source ambiguity. The original states orthogonal without explicit unit lengths, but its sum omits squared-norm denominators. No unique literal key is asserted. The answer separates the literal wording from an added orthonormal interpretation and handles the full-space boundary.
1.

P is idempotent.

2.

If x∈U then Px∈U.

3.

For every x, ‖x‖2≤‖Px‖2.

4.

P is a linear operator from ℝm to U.

Read the complete derivation, checks, and diagnosed alternatives

Source ambiguity; intended normalized interpretation: option 3.

Read the source hypothesis literally

The original Persian page says “orthogonal basis” and does not explicitly state unit lengths. Orthogonal and orthonormal are different hypotheses. For a nonunit orthogonal basis, the correct orthogonal projection formula is

PUx=∑k=1n⟨uk,x⟩⟨uk,uk⟩uk.

The source omits these denominators. To see why this matters, take U=span(2,0) in ℝ2. Its displayed operator is Ps=diag(4,0), whereas the actual orthogonal projection is diag(1,0). Applying Ps twice gives diag(16,0), so option 1's idempotence assertion fails. For x=(0,1), Psx=0 and option 3's inequality is also false. Thus the literal hypothesis does not supply one uniquely false general assertion. No official answer key is asserted here.

If “orthogonal” was intended to include normalization in the source convention, the extra orthonormal hypothesis gives the usual educational answer, option 3. The following proof states that interpretation explicitly rather than silently changing the authentic wording.

Under the orthonormal interpretation

Let p=Px and r=x−p. For each basis vector uj, orthonormality gives

⟨r,uj⟩=⟨x,uj⟩−∑k=1n⟨x,uk⟩⟨uk,uj⟩=0.

Thus p∈U and r⊥U. Pythagoras proves ‖x‖22=‖Px‖22+‖x−Px‖22. The universally valid direction is ‖Px‖2≤‖x‖2, with equality precisely when x∈U. The reverse inequality fails on a proper subspace: for U=span(1,0) and x=(0,1), it reads 1≤0.

Linearity of the coefficient functionals gives option 4, and outputs lie in U by construction. For x∈U, the orthonormal expansion recovers x, proving option 2 and the stronger Px=x. Applying this fact to Px∈U proves P2=P, option 1.

Full-space boundary. The source allows n=m. With an orthonormal basis of the entire space, P=I, so option 3 holds with equality and all four assertions hold for that particular configuration. It is false as a general projection theorem, not false for every possible subspace or vector.

Finally, idempotence alone does not imply contraction: Q=(1200) has Q2=Q but sends (0,1) to (2,0). Orthogonality supplies the norm decomposition; a projection must be identified by its actual geometry and formula.

Exact verification ledger

Hypothesis Displayed sum idempotent? Reverse norm inequality
Literal nonunit orthogonal basis Not generally; u=(2,0) disproves it. Not generally; a perpendicular input disproves it.
Orthonormal basis of a proper subspace Yes Fails on a nonzero perpendicular vector.
Orthonormal basis of the full space Yes; P=I Equality for every vector.

The model declares its exact matrix data and demonstrates the corresponding operation.

Question 5. PhD CS 1404, Q32 — A matrix parameter range

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 8 · question 32. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

The symmetric 3×3 matrix has diagonal entries 1 and every off-diagonal entry a. For which range of a is it positive definite?

1.
−1<a<1
2.
−1/2<a<1
3.
−1/2<a<1/2
4.
0<a<1
Read the complete derivation, checks, and diagnosed alternatives

Correct option: 2.

The source matrix is A=(1−a)I+a11T in three dimensions. Every real vector can be written uniquely as x=s1+z, with s=(x1+x2+x3)/3 and z1+z2+z3=0. The two terms are orthogonal. Expanding the quadratic form gives

xTAx=3(1+2a)s2+(1−a)‖z‖22.

If a≥1, choose nonzero z=(1,−1,0) and s=0; the form is nonpositive. If a≤−1/2, choose s=1,z=0; again the form is nonpositive. Thus strict positive definiteness requires 1−a>0 and 1+2a>0.

Conversely, if both coefficients are positive, every nonzero x has either s≠0 or z≠0, and the displayed sum is strictly positive. This proves sufficiency directly, without importing an unexplained eigenvalue criterion. The exact interval is −1/2<a<1, option 2.

Option 1 permits, for example, a=−3/4, where the all-equal direction gives 3(1+2a)=−3/2. Option 3 unnecessarily rejects a=3/4, where both coefficients are positive. Option 4 unnecessarily rejects a=−1/4, also valid, and excludes a=0, the identity matrix. At a=−1/2, the all-equal line is null; at a=1, the sum-zero plane is null. Both endpoints are positive semidefinite but not positive definite. Outside the closed interval, a direction of negative quadratic form exists.

For n≥2 with the analogous real symmetric matrix, the decomposition yields coefficients 1+(n−1)a and 1−a, hence strict range −1/(n−1)<a<1. At n=1, there are no off-diagonal entries: the matrix is simply (1) and places no restriction on the unused parameter. The special dimension-one case must not be inferred by dividing by zero in the general endpoint.

The model declares its exact matrix data and demonstrates the corresponding operation.

Question 6. A scalar identity plus an all-ones matrix — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Original authored matrix-algebra question; no specific authentic source item is asserted for this mechanism.

Let J be the all-ones n -by- n matrix. Find det(I+J). Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

Prove the all-equal and sum-zero decomposition, justify the determinant computation, and independently verify a closed-form inverse. Test the smallest dimension and distinguish a sufficient triangular guarantee from a numerical coincidence.

1.
32
2.
5
3.
1
4.
6
Read the complete derivation, checks, and diagnosed alternatives

Correct option: 4.

Construct the result from the defining map

Let q=(1,…,1)T and J=qqT. For every vector x,

Jx=(∑i=1nxi)q,Jq=nq.

Write x=sq+z with s=(∑ixi)/n and ∑izi=0. This decomposition is unique because the all-equal line intersects the sum-zero subspace only at zero over the real field. The vectors ei−en, 1≤i<n, form a basis of the latter: their first n−1 coordinates prove independence and reconstruct every sum-zero vector. In this adapted basis, I+J is diagonal with entries n+1,1,…,1. Consequently

det(I+J)=(n+1)·1n−1=n+1.

The determinant's invariance under an invertible basis change follows from multiplicativity: det(S−1MS)=det(S)−1det(M)det(S). We are not multiplying the diagonal of the original dense matrix. All of its diagonal entries are two, whose product 2n is generally wrong.

A direct inverse provides an independent structural check. Since J2=nJ,

(I+J)(I−Jn+1)=I+J−Jn+1−nJn+1=I.

The reverse product agrees because these factors are polynomials in J. Thus singularity of the addend J for n>1 does not make I+J singular.

Exact answer, competing options, and boundary

At n=5, the adapted-basis entries are 6,1,1,1,1, so the determinant is 6, option 4. The alternatives 32, 5 and 1 respectively multiply the original diagonal, omit the added identity on the all-equal line, or ignore that line's changed scale. A matrix can have every displayed diagonal entry equal to two yet determinant six; the other entries participate in its volume transformation.

The model declares its exact matrix data and demonstrates the corresponding operation.

An inverse verified by finite cancellation

Question 10. An inverse verified by finite cancellation — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Original authored matrix-algebra question; no specific authentic source item is asserted for this mechanism.

Invert the two-by-two matrix with diagonal entries one, lower-left entry zero, and upper-right entry n. Find the upper-right entry of its inverse. Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

Verify the inverse on both sides and through the actual shear action. Extend to a three-step nilpotent and a compatible rectangular coupling block; state every denominator assumption.

1.
−5
2.
5
3.
15
4.
0
Read the complete derivation, checks, and diagnosed alternatives

Correct option: 1.

Construct the result from the defining map

Write the shear as S=I+N, where

S=(1n01),N=(0n00),N2=0.

Both ordered products satisfy (I+N)(I−N)=(I−N)(I+N)=I−N2=I, proving

S−1=(1−n01).

On a vector (x,y)T, the first map outputs (x+ny,y)T; the inverse must subtract precisely the same multiple of the unchanged second coordinate. This explains the negative upper-right entry geometrically. Entrywise reciprocation is unrelated to undoing a map and is already undefined at the zero entries of this invertible matrix.

More generally, a nilpotent matrix N with Nr=0 gives a finite inverse polynomial

(I+N)−1=∑j=0r−1(−1)jNj.

Multiplication cancels adjacent terms and leaves I+(−1)r−1Nr=I in either order. No infinite geometric-series convergence assumption is used. If N3=0 rather than N2=0, the extra N2 term is necessary; simply negating all off-diagonal entries can fail.

Exact answer, competing options, and boundary

At n=5, the answer is −5, option 1. Substituting the candidates into an alleged inverse X=(1t01) gives (SX)12=5+t. Values 5,1/5,0 leave 10,26/5,5, respectively; only t=−5 makes this entry zero. The reverse product has the same scalar sum, so both sides are certified.

A diagonal matrix times a cyclic permutation

Question 14. A diagonal matrix times a cyclic permutation — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Original authored matrix-algebra question; no specific authentic source item is asserted for this mechanism.

Let A=diag(1,2,…,n) and let P cyclically shift all n standard coordinates, with no fixed coordinate. Find tr(AP). Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

Derive the trace from weighted fixed coordinates. Compare a derangement with a permutation having a fixed point, then prove cyclic trace invariance without assuming multiplicativity.

The factor premises require n≥2.

1.
5
2.
25
3.
0
4.
15
Read the complete derivation, checks, and diagnosed alternatives

Correct option: 3.

Construct the result from the defining map

Use D=diag(1,2,…,n) with n≥2 and a permutation matrix P having no fixed coordinate. The entry formula, not a rule about trace multiplicativity, gives

(DP)ii=∑kDikPki=iPii.

Only k=i survives because D is diagonal. A permutation diagonal entry Pii equals one exactly when the permutation fixes coordinate i. Therefore

tr(DP)=∑i:Pii=1i=0.

For an arbitrary diagonal weight matrix and arbitrary permutation, the same derivation gives the sum of weights on the fixed coordinates. The no-fixed-coordinate hypothesis is doing real work. Multiplying on the left rescales rows but cannot change a zero diagonal entry into a nonzero one.

Cyclic trace invariance is a different theorem. For compatible rectangular matrices A,B,

tr(AB)=∑i∑jaijbji=∑j∑ibjiaij=tr(BA).

The scalar terms commute inside the sums; the matrices need not commute. For three factors the allowed operation rotates the entire sequence. It does not allow arbitrary factor swapping or removal.

Exact answer, competing options, and boundary

At n=5, all five diagonal entries of DP are zero, giving option 3. The alternatives 5,25,15 respectively suggest a coordinate count, a squared size, or tr(D)=1+2+3+4+5. None computes iPii. To audit the premise, write the actual cycle e1↦e2↦…↦e5↦e1; no diagonal entry receives a one.

The model declares its exact matrix data and demonstrates the corresponding operation.

For A=2I and B=3I in dimension n, find det(AB). Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

Derive the dimensional determinant power and diagnose determinant-versus-trace and product-versus-sum errors. Include noncommuting factors in the scope argument.

Read the complete derivation, checks, and diagnosed alternatives

Correct option: 2.

Construct the result from the defining map

The two factors are 2In and 3In, so their product is 6In. Every diagonal entry is six and all off-diagonal entries are zero. Thus

det((2In)(3In))=det(6In)=6n.

This is a legitimate diagonal-product computation because the matrix is diagonal. It can also be derived by determinant multiplicativity: det(2In)det(3In)=2n3n. No commutation hypothesis is required by determinant multiplicativity, although these particular diagonal factors do commute.

The dimension exponent has a geometric and algebraic meaning. Scaling the whole matrix by c scales each of its n rows. Multilinearity of determinant extracts one scalar from each row:

det(cA)=cndet(A).

The determinant measures oriented n -dimensional volume, while trace adds n diagonal values. Their scaling laws are different: tr(cA)=ctr(A). A matrix power with a second-superdiagonal term

Question 22. A matrix power with a second-superdiagonal term — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Original authored matrix-algebra question; no specific authentic source item is asserted for this mechanism.

Let N be the three-by-three matrix with ones immediately above its diagonal and zeros elsewhere. Find entry (1,3) of (I+N)n. Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

Explain the coefficient using distinct chronological move slots and independently derive its recurrence. Extend to weighted direct and indirect paths and test powers zero and one.

1.
25
2.
15
3.
10
4.
5
Read the complete derivation, checks, and diagnosed alternatives

Correct option: 3.

Construct the result from the defining map

Let N have N12=N23=1 and all other entries zero. Acting on the coordinate basis gives Ne3=e2, Ne2=e1 and Ne1=0. Thus N2=E13 and N3=0. Since identity commutes with N, the binomial expansion terminates:

(I+N)k=I+kN+(k2)N2=(1k(k2)01k001),k≥0.

The (1,3) coefficient uses two distinct time slots. At one slot the action moves e3 to e2; at a later slot it moves e2 to e1. The remaining slots apply identity. There are (k2) choices of the ordered pair of distinct slots once their chronological order is fixed. Allowing a double move inside one factor would count an operation that I+N does not perform.

An independent recurrence verifies the same result. If tk denotes the upper-right coefficient, multiplying the displayed power by I+N gives

tk+1=tk+k,t0=0,

so tk=0+1+…+(k−1)=k(k−1)/2. This recurrence explains every checkpoint of the associated path simulation.

Exact answer, competing options, and boundary

For exponent five, the answer is 5·4/2=10, option 3. The incorrect 25 counts two slots independently with replacement and order; 15 uses 1+…+5 instead of 0+…+4; five is the first-superdiagonal coefficient, which needs only one move. A state ledger at powers 0,1,2,3,4,5 gives upper-right values 0,0,1,3,6,10, with increments 0,1,2,3,4.

The model declares its exact matrix data and demonstrates the corresponding operation.

Correct option: 4.

Construct the result from the defining map

Let N have N12=N23=1 and all other entries zero. Acting on the coordinate basis gives Ne3=e2, Ne2=e1 and Ne1=0. Thus N2=E13 and N3=0. Since identity commutes with N, the binomial expansion terminates:

(I+N)k=I+kN+(k2)N2=(1k(k2)01k001),k≥0.

Option 4 identifies why the standard binomial grouping is justified here: the summands I and N commute. For arbitrary square matrices, (A+B)2=A2+AB+BA+B2, and replacing the middle terms by 2AB requires AB=BA. Choose A=diag(1,0), B=E12: AB=B but BA=0, so the ordinary scalar square formula is false. Nilpotence does not mean the matrix itself is zero; our N is a direct counterexample. The first- and second-power coefficients differ, as exponent five gives five versus ten. Coincidences at an isolated exponent do not establish a universal expansion.

A full-column factor followed by a full-row factor

Question 26. A full-column factor followed by a full-row factor — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Original authored matrix-algebra question; no specific authentic source item is asserted for this mechanism.

An n -by-two matrix U has rank two, and a two-by- n matrix V has rank two. Find rank(UV). Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

Prove image equality using the onto first action and injective second action, not merely a rank upper bound. Compare the reverse product and the n=2 boundary.

The factor premises require n≥2.

1.
2
2.
5
3.
4
4.
0
Read the complete derivation, checks, and diagnosed alternatives

Correct option: 1.

Construct the result from the defining map

Let U have shape n×2 and rank two, and V shape 2×n and rank two, with n≥2. The map V:ℝn→ℝ2 is onto because its image has the full codomain dimension two. The map U:ℝ2→ℝn is injective because its kernel has dimension 2−2=0. Therefore

im(UV)=U(imV)=U(ℝ2)=imU,rank(UV)=2.

This proves equality, not merely an upper bound. Equivalently, UVx=0 implies Vx=0 by injectivity of U, so ker(UV)=kerV and the nullity is n−2.

For a general product AB, one only has rank(AB)≤min(rankA,rankB) without additional hypotheses. If A=diag(1,0) and B=diag(0,1), both factors have rank one but AB=0. The first factor kills the entire image of the second. The original problem avoids that loss because the left factor is injective on its whole two-dimensional domain.

Exact answer, competing options, and boundary

At n=5, the square product has rank two, option 1, and kernel dimension three. Its being five-by-five does not imply rank five; there are only two intermediate coordinates. Rank four wrongly adds factor ranks; rank zero contradicts the injective-left/onto-right composition argument. A concrete witness is U=[e1e2] and V=UT, giving UV=diag(1,1,0,0,0).

The model declares its exact matrix data and demonstrates the corresponding operation.

Question 30. A change of basis and an off-diagonal coefficient — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Original authored matrix-algebra question; no specific authentic source item is asserted for this mechanism.

A linear map has standard matrix diag(2,n). Use ordered basis (1,1),(1,−1). Find its first-row, second-column matrix entry in that basis. Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

Reconstruct each transformed basis image and solve its actual coefficient equations. State that the same ordered basis is used on both sides; distinguish independent input/output conversions.

1.

2.
3

Read the complete derivation, checks, and diagnosed alternatives

Correct option: 3.

Construct the result from the defining map

Use the ordered basis B=(b1,b2) with b1=(1,1)T, b2=(1,−1)T, and the standard-coordinate map T=diag(2,n). The basis matrix and its inverse are

B=(111−1),B−1=12B.

For a basis-coordinate input c, the conversion sequence is c↦Bc↦TBc↦B−1TBc. Hence

[T]B=B−1TB=12(n+22−n2−nn+2).

The first-row second-column entry is the first basis coefficient of T(b2)=(2,−n)T. Solve c1+c2=2 and c1−c2=−n; adding yields c1=(2−n)/2, and subtracting yields c2=(2+n)/2. This column construction independently verifies the conjugation calculation.

The same ordered basis is used on input and output because T is an endomorphism. Independent basis choices would instead give C−1TB, not necessarily a similarity. Under similarity, trace and determinant remain n+2 and 2n, while individual entries generally change. These invariants are useful checks, not replacements for converting the actual columns.

Exact answer, competing options, and boundary

At n=5, the transformed matrix is (7/2−3/2−3/27/2). The answer is −3/2, option 3. Values −3, three and 7/2 omit the half factor, reverse the sign while omitting it, or give the diagonal coefficient instead. Reconstructing the second image gives (−3/2)b1+(7/2)b2=(2,−5)T, exactly T(b2).

The model declares its exact matrix data and demonstrates the corresponding operation.

The answer is (2−n)/2, option 1. The plus expression gives the other coefficient of the same image; the remaining differences omit basis normalization and sometimes change sign. At n≠2, the displayed two eigenvectors mix the original coordinate axes, which generally creates off-diagonal entries.

(AC0D)−1=(A−1−A−1CD−10D−1).

At n=5, the determinant is 25=32, option 1. Values one, ten and 1024 ignore the second diagonal block, confuse the dimension-dependent product with 2n, or compute 45 as if all ten diagonal coordinates were scaled by two. Exactly five coordinates contribute a factor two; the first five contribute one.

Question 38. Dimension with a second independent constraint

2.

14

3.

13

4.
